393.title: Gideon's fleece (Judges 6–7)
393.hook: the least in his family asks for signs and wins with 300
393.howItsDone: Catholics hear Gideon's call in the Mass readings, and in traditional Marian devotion the dew-soaked fleece is honored as a figure of Mary and the Incarnation, drawn from the Church Fathers and old Advent hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Deborah under her palm, and a commander who wouldn't go without her. Your line was she judged israel.

A young man is threshing wheat in a winepress. That's an odd place for it; you thresh on an open hilltop where the wind can carry the chaff away. But raiders from Midian have been stripping the land every harvest, so he's hiding, beating out a little grain in a pit. That's where an angel finds him, sits down under an oak, and greets him with a line that sounds almost like a joke: "The Lord is with thee, O most valiant of men." The most valiant of men is crouched in a pit, hiding his wheat. His name is Gideon, Gedeon in the Douay-Rheims.
screen: `THRESHING WHEAT IN A WINEPRESS.` → `HIDING FROM THE RAIDERS.` → `O MOST VALIANT OF MEN.`

segments.voice: Gideon doesn't believe it. He says, in the Douay: "Behold my family is the meanest in Manasses, and I am the least in my father's house." And he wants proof. He lays a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asks God for dew on the fleece only, with the ground dry. In the morning he wrings out a bowl of water. Then, nervously, he asks for the reverse: dry fleece, wet ground. God does that too, and the text doesn't scold him for asking. Now the army. Gideon gathers thirty-two thousand men, and God says: too many. The reason is blunt: "lest Israel should glory against me, and say: I was delivered by my own strength." Twenty-two thousand go home. Ten thousand left, still too many. At the water, God sets apart the three hundred who lap. Some sermons say they were picked for being alert; the text never says that. They're simply fewer. With trumpets, clay jars and torches, three hundred men throw a vast camp into panic in the night. And Catholics have a second way of seeing the fleece. Early Christian writers, Saint Ambrose among them, saw in the dew falling on the fleece alone a figure of the Incarnation, God's gift coming down quietly on one woman, Mary. Some Catholic readers also hear in the angel's greeting, the Lord is with thee, an echo of Gabriel's. The thread through it all: God picks the least, and trims the army, so nobody can mistake who won.
screen: `THE LEAST IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE.` · `DEW ON THE FLEECE, THEN DRY.` · `THIRTY-TWO THOUSAND TO THREE HUNDRED.` · `THE FATHERS SAW MARY IN THE DEW.` · then, large: `I WAS DELIVERED BY MY OWN STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you feel short: not enough time, money, people or patience. Imagine the number going down, the way Gideon's did, and ask what you could still do with what's left: one hour used well, one friend, one honest try. If you pray, hand that small number to God the way Gideon held out his fleece.
Gideon's fleece. The sign a frightened judge asked for, twice, and was given. In English, putting out a fleece has come to mean asking God for a sign. Today's word.
Your line: fewer is enough. Three hundred men were plenty. That's day three hundred ninety-three.

394.title: Samson (Judges 13–16)
394.hook: great strength, poor choices, and one last prayer
394.howItsDone: Catholics hear the announcement of Samson's birth at daily Mass in late Advent, paired with the angel's announcement of John the Baptist's birth, and the Church reads his life as a warning as much as an example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon's fleece and an army of three hundred. Your line was fewer is enough.

A few days before Christmas, the weekday Mass reading sounds almost like a Gospel. A woman who has no children is visited by a messenger of God. You will conceive and bear a son, he tells her, and no razor will touch his head; he'll be set apart for God from his mother's womb. That child grows up astonishingly strong. He tears a lion apart with his hands and carries off a city's gates. And he makes one wrong choice after another. His name is Samson.
screen: `A READING BEFORE CHRISTMAS.` → `NO RAZOR SHALL TOUCH HIS HEAD.` → `STRONG, AND CHOOSING BADLY.`

segments.voice: Samson is a Nazarite, Nazirite elsewhere: someone consecrated to God, who drinks no wine and never cuts his hair. The long hair is the sign of the vow; the strength is God's gift. Keep those two apart, because Samson doesn't. He marries outside his people against his parents' pleading. He sets three hundred foxes loose with torches in the enemy's fields. He's ruled by appetite and revenge. Then Delilah. Three times she asks what makes him strong, three times he lies, and three times the Philistines burst in. The fourth time he tells her the truth, in the Douay-Rheims: "if my head be shaven, my strength shall depart from me." She lulls him to sleep on her knees, calls a barber, and his seven locks are shaved. He wakes and thinks he'll shake himself free as before, "not knowing that the Lord was departed from him." The hair wasn't magic. Some readers see it as the last piece of a vow he had been bending all along. Blinded and chained, he grinds grain in a prison, and his hair starts to grow. At a feast for their god, they bring him out to mock him, and he prays: "O Lord God, remember me, and restore to me now my former strength." The rest of the prayer, the text admits, asks revenge for his eyes. He pushes the pillars, and the house falls on him and on them. The Church doesn't hold Samson up as a model of virtue, but the Letter to the Hebrews names him among the people of faith. Strength never made Samson wise. At the end, it was a prayer that made him remember who his strength belonged to.
screen: `A NAZARITE: SET APART FOR GOD.` · `STRONG, AND RULED BY APPETITE.` · `THE LORD WAS DEPARTED FROM HIM.` · `REMEMBER ME, O LORD GOD.` · then, large: `RESTORE TO ME NOW MY FORMER STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Samson's trouble wasn't a lack of strength but a soft spot he kept walking back into: flattery, anger, wanting what he wanted. Name yours quietly, and look at it the way you'd look at a door you keep leaving unlocked. If you pray, borrow Samson's words, O Lord God, remember me; if not, just look, without excuses.

395.title: Whither thou goest (Ruth 1)
395.hook: a Moabite widow refuses to leave her mother-in-law: thy people shall be my people
395.howItsDone: Catholics hear Ruth's story in the weekday Mass readings, and hear her name again in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, where she stands among his ancestors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson, undone by his own choices and saved at the end by a prayer. Your line was strength isn't wisdom.

Three widows stand on a road. One is old: Naomi, Noemi in the Douay-Rheims. She left Bethlehem in a famine with her husband and two sons, and in the land of Moab she lost all three. The other two are young Moabite women who married her sons. Now Naomi is walking home with nothing, and she tells them: go back to your mothers. I have no more sons for you. They cry. One of them, Orpah, kisses her and turns back, and nobody in the story blames her. The other one won't let go. Her name is Ruth.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `GO HOME TO YOUR MOTHERS.` → `ONE TURNS BACK. ONE WON'T.`

segments.voice: What Ruth says next has traveled far beyond this book. In older English it's remembered as whither thou goest, I will go. The Douay-Rheims gives it like this: "whithersoever thou shalt go, I will go: and where thou shalt dwell, I also will dwell. Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." She goes further: where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried. Notice who she's saying it to. Not a husband. A mother-in-law, old, grieving and broke, who has just told her to leave. Some couples choose these words for their weddings, but first they were a daughter-in-law's vow to a widow with nothing to offer. The Hebrew storytellers have a word for what Ruth does: chesed, steady, loyal love that keeps showing up. Naomi even uses it on the road, praying that God will deal kindly with the two young women, as they have dealt with the dead and with her. Ruth is a foreigner, from Moab, a people Israel had old quarrels with, and she becomes, in this book, the picture of faithfulness. In Bethlehem the town women say, is this Naomi? And Naomi answers, in the Douay: "I went out full, and the Lord hath brought me back empty." Don't call me Naomi, she says, which means beautiful. Call me Mara, bitter. The book lets her say it. It doesn't correct her or rush her. It just keeps Ruth standing beside her, through the bitterness, at the start of the barley harvest.
screen: `WHITHER THOU GOEST, I WILL GO.` · `A VOW TO A MOTHER-IN-LAW.` · `CHESED — LOVE THAT STAYS.` · `CALL ME MARA, BITTER.` · then, large: `THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who is grieving right now, a death, a divorce, a diagnosis, a move they didn't want, maybe someone who, like Naomi, has told everyone to go away. Picture yourself on the road beside them, not fixing anything, just walking. If you pray, hold them before God by name; if not, simply stay beside them in your mind a while.
chesed. Hebrew for steady, loyal love that keeps showing up, the word for Ruth's promise to Naomi, a widow who had nothing left. Today's word.
Your line: thy people, my people. Loyal love doesn't wait to be asked. See you tomorrow.

396.title: Gleaning (Ruth 2–4)
396.hook: Boaz leaves extra grain on purpose, and Ruth becomes David's great-grandmother
396.howItsDone: Catholics hear Ruth's story in the weekday Mass readings, and some Catholic charities and parish food ministries point to gleaning as a model of caring for the poor while protecting their dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth's chesed on the road to Bethlehem: whither thou goest, I will go. Your line was thy people, my people.

There's no food in the house. Naomi and Ruth have reached Bethlehem with nothing, just as the barley harvest begins. So Ruth does what the poor did in Israel: she goes out behind the reapers and picks up what they drop. The law of Moses said farmers must not strip their fields bare; leave the edges and what falls for the poor and the stranger, a safety net built into the harvest. Ruth is both poor and a stranger. And the field she happens to walk into belongs to Boaz, Booz in the Douay-Rheims, a relative of Naomi's dead husband.
screen: `NO FOOD IN THE HOUSE.` → `LEAVE THE EDGES FOR THE POOR.` → `A FIELD THAT BELONGS TO BOAZ.`

segments.voice: Gleaning means gathering what's left after the harvest: the stray ears of grain, the leftovers, the edges. It's slow, bent-over work, the work of people with nothing else. Boaz walks out, sees the foreign woman, and asks who she is. He's already heard everything she did for her mother-in-law. So he protects her: stay in my field, drink from my workers' water jars, eat with us at mealtime. Then he quietly tells his young men, in the Douay: "let fall some of your handfuls of purpose, and leave them, that she may gather them without shame." Of purpose. He doesn't hand her a sack of grain like a charity case. He arranges the field so her own work finds more, and her dignity stays whole. That evening she beats out about an ephah of barley. In the chapters that follow, Naomi sends Ruth to Boaz at the threshing floor, and Boaz acts as the go'el, the kinsman who redeems a family's land and name. He marries Ruth. They have a son, Obed. And the book ends with a short family tree: Obed is the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David. A foreign widow who gathered leftovers becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Catholics hear one more step: when Matthew's Gospel opens with Jesus's family tree, Ruth is named in it, one of only a few women listed. Kindness on purpose, in one barley field, runs all the way to Bethlehem again.
screen: `GLEANING — GATHERING WHAT'S LEFT.` · `LET FALL SOME HANDFULS ON PURPOSE.` · `BOAZ, THE KINSMAN WHO REDEEMS.` · `GREAT-GRANDMOTHER OF DAVID.` · then, large: `THAT SHE MAY GATHER THEM WITHOUT SHAME.`

segments.voice: Think about where your own field has edges: the extra in the grocery cart, the tip, the parking spot near the door, the credit for an idea. Pick one place you could let something fall on purpose, so someone else can pick it up without feeling handed charity, and picture doing it quietly, the way Boaz did. If you pray, ask for eyes like his.
Gleaning. Gathering the grain left behind after harvest, which the law left for the poor and the stranger. Ruth gleaned in the field of Boaz. Today's word.
Your line: kindness on purpose. Boaz made sure it looked like her own harvest. Day three hundred ninety-six.

397.title: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1–2)
397.hook: a woman prays so hard the priest thinks she's drunk, then sings like Mary will
397.howItsDone: Catholics pray Hannah's song as one of the Old Testament canticles in the Liturgy of the Hours, at Morning Prayer, and many couples hoping for a child find company in her story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gleaning: grain dropped on purpose for Ruth. Your line was kindness on purpose.

Every year a family travels up to the sanctuary at Shiloh, and every year it's the worst week for one of them. Her name is Hannah, Anna in the Douay-Rheims. Her husband loves her, but she has no children, and his other wife has many and needles her about it, year after year, until Hannah can't eat. Her husband tries to help: Am I not better to thee than ten children? It doesn't help. So one year, after the meal, she goes to the doorway of the house of the Lord and starts to pray. An old priest named Eli is sitting there on a stool, watching.
screen: `THE YEARLY TRIP TO SHILOH.` → `NO CHILDREN, AND A RIVAL'S TAUNTS.` → `AN OLD PRIEST ON A STOOL, WATCHING.`

segments.voice: Hannah prays with tears. Her lips move, but no sound comes out. People usually prayed aloud then, so to Eli she looks drunk. He tells her to go sleep it off. She answers him, in the Douay: "I am an exceeding unhappy woman, and have drunk neither wine nor any strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the Lord." Not a polite request: everything in her, poured out. And Eli, to his credit, changes his tune: go in peace, and may God grant your petition. After that, the text says, her face was no longer sad. Nothing has happened yet. She simply prayed and was heard. Then she has a son, Samuel, and when he's weaned she brings him back to Shiloh and gives him to the Lord's service, just as she vowed. And she sings: "My heart hath rejoiced in the Lord." Her song turns the world upside down: the mighty are broken, the weak are girded with strength, the hungry are filled, and God lifts the poor from the dust to sit with princes. Centuries later, a young woman named Mary visits her cousin and sings: my soul doth magnify the Lord, he hath put down the mighty and exalted the humble, filled the hungry with good things. The Church has long heard Hannah's song as the older sister of Mary's Magnificat, and prays it among the Old Testament canticles in the Liturgy of the Hours.
screen: `LIPS MOVING, NO SOUND.` · `I HAVE POURED OUT MY SOUL.` · `HER FACE WAS NO MORE SAD.` · `A SONG THAT MARY WILL ECHO.` · then, large: `MY HEART HATH REJOICED IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of what you've carried the longest, the ache you don't bring up anymore because people are tired of hearing it, or you are, and don't tidy it. If you pray, tell God exactly how it is, silently, the way Hannah did, with no polite words in front; if not, say it plainly to yourself. Then stay a moment, and notice your face.

398.title: Speak, Lord (1 Samuel 3)
398.hook: a boy wakes three times to a voice and learns to say speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth
398.howItsDone: Some Catholics use Samuel's words, speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth, as a short prayer before reading scripture or in quiet adoration, and the chapter is read on a Sunday in Ordinary Time alongside the call of the first disciples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah at Shiloh, praying so hard the priest thought she was drunk. Your line was she poured out her soul. Today, the boy she prayed for.

It's the middle of the night in the sanctuary at Shiloh. The lamp of God hasn't gone out yet. An old priest, Eli, is asleep in his place; his eyes have grown so dim he can barely see. A boy is asleep near the ark of God: Samuel, Hannah's son, the one she gave to the Lord. The text adds a sad note about those days: the word of the Lord was rare, and visions were few. Then, in the dark, someone calls the boy's name. Samuel runs to the old man. Here I am. You called me. Eli rolls over: I didn't call you. Go back to sleep.
screen: `NIGHT AT SHILOH.` → `THE WORD OF THE LORD WAS RARE.` → `HERE I AM. YOU CALLED ME.`

segments.voice: It happens again, and then a third time. And the text gives the reason he keeps getting it wrong: "Samuel did not yet know the Lord." He's grown up in the house of God, serves there every day, and doesn't recognize God's voice. That isn't a failure. He's simply young. On the third time, the old man understands. Eli, who has his own failings, and whose sons have been a disgrace, still knows this much: it's God. So he gives the boy one line to say. In the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." Samuel lies down again, and the text says the Lord came and stood, and called as before: Samuel, Samuel. This time the boy says it. Notice what the line does. Speak comes first: Samuel asks for the word. Then heareth: he promises to listen. In Hebrew, heareth is the same verb as the Shema's hear, the hear, O Israel this path met not long ago. And what God says is hard: judgment on Eli's house. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell him. Eli insists, and Samuel tells him everything. Hearing God can mean carrying a message you'd rather not. The Church reads this chapter at Sunday Mass beside the call of Jesus's first disciples in John's Gospel. And some Catholics pray speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth as a whole prayer, with no other words.

399.title: Saul, head and shoulders taller (1 Samuel 9–10)
399.hook: the first king is chosen, hiding among the baggage
399.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Saul's anointing in the weekday Mass readings, and the Church's own anointings, at baptism, confirmation and ordination with sacred chrism, carry on the old sign of oil poured on someone chosen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy at Shiloh learning to say speak, Lord. Your line was thy servant heareth.

A farmer's donkeys have wandered off. He sends his son and a servant to find them, and they search the hill country for three days. They're about to go home when the servant says: there's a man of God in the next town. Maybe he can tell us where the donkeys went. So a tall young man walks into town looking for lost animals, and walks out a king. The man of God is Samuel, now grown old. The young man is Saul. The Bible says there was no goodlier person among the children of Israel; from his shoulders upward he stood above everyone.
screen: `THE LOST DONKEYS.` → `ASK THE MAN OF GOD.` → `LOOKING FOR ANIMALS, FOUND A CROWN.`

segments.voice: Israel had asked Samuel for a king, to be like the nations around them, and the text treats it as a sad request: they're setting aside God as their king. God tells Samuel to give them one anyway. Before Saul can even ask about the donkeys, Samuel tells him: they're found, stop worrying. Then, privately, he pours a little vial of oil on Saul's head and kisses him. The Lord has anointed you prince over his people. Anointed: in Hebrew, mashiach, the word English borrows as Messiah; Greek translates it Christ. At its start, it's simply oil on a nervous young man's head. When Samuel first hints at greatness, Saul answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Am not I a son of Jemini of the least tribe of Israel?" Benjamin, the smallest tribe. Then the public choosing. All Israel gathers, lots are cast, tribe by tribe, family by family, and the lot falls on Saul. Everyone turns to look, and he isn't there. In the Hebrew, the Lord's answer is: he has hidden himself among the baggage. The Douay, following the Latin, says only: "Behold he is hidden at home." Either way, the man who stands taller than everyone is crouched out of sight. They pull him out, and the people shout: "God save the king." A tender, almost funny beginning; the story will darken: Saul's reign ends in jealousy and tragedy. But this week has been full of people who felt too small: Gideon in the winepress, Ruth the stranger, Hannah in tears, a boy in the dark. Saul makes one more.
screen: `ISRAEL ASKS FOR A KING.` · `OIL ON HIS HEAD: ANOINTED.` · `THE LEAST TRIBE OF ISRAEL.` · `HIDING AMONG THE BAGGAGE.` · then, large: `GOD SAVE THE KING.`

segments.voice: Saul hid at the exact moment he was called. Think of where you duck out of sight when asked to stand up, busyness, jokes, your phone, letting someone louder go first, and notice it without judging. Then picture stepping out, the way Saul finally did, and if you pray, ask for that courage.
Saul. Israel's first king, tall and frightened, anointed by Samuel and found hiding among the baggage. Today's word.
Your line: hiding in the baggage. And that's week fifty-seven: Gideon's fleece, Samson, Ruth on the road, gleaning, Hannah's prayer, speak, Lord, and Saul. Day three hundred ninety-nine, done.
